result.abstractText: Our reliance on honey bees (Apis mellifera) for pollination services and honey production continues to increase due to the global decline in other pollinators and rising demand for honey. The ectoparasitic mite (Varroa destructor) remains the biggest pest of honey bees forcing beekeepers into continual miticide use. Beekeepers on the Tibetan Plateau, however, report rarely seeing mites in their colonies, unlike all other areas of China. We conducted a series of translocation experiments to investigate this phenomenon. Here, we show that hypoxic conditions above 3,500 m on the Tibetan Plateau reduce mite fecundity and arrest offspring development, and so prevent the long-term persistence of the mite population. This reduced mite fertility and arrested offspring development were also found in honey bee colonies maintained at low altitude but under hypoxic conditions like those found at 3,500 m. This discovery of a physiological limit to V. destructor reproduction highlights a previously unrecognized sensitivity of this mite to reduced oxygen availability, the mechanistic basis of which warrants further investigation. This discovery could unlock new chemical-free innovative mite-control methods that will benefit both the beekeeping industry and help ensure food security.

result.title: Male bumblebees are capable of providing brood care and impacting nest development in incipient nests.

authorAffiliation.affiliation: Department of Entomology, University of California, Riverside, CA, USA.
Department of Entomology, University of California, Riverside, CA, USA.

result.abstractText: Brood care is a core component of some social systems and a defining feature of eusocial insects. A recurring theme in eusocial Hymenoptera is that males are non-contributing members of social groups. Males are instead viewed solely as reproductives who leave their natal nest shortly after emergence to mate, then die thereafter. There is, however, some evidence across eusocial hymenopteran lineages that males do contribute to the nest. Here, we show that in the bumblebee Bombus impatiens, males incubate developing brood in lab-reared nests, and the presence of males positively contributes to nest development during the early nesting stage. We further demonstrate that in contrast to queens, males maintain a greater heat differential between the thorax and abdomen during incubation, suggesting sex-specific differences in thermal regulation. Our findings add to the evidence that males incubate in lab-reared bumblebee nests and expand this to demonstrate that there is an impact on nest initiation and development.

result.abstractText: The physiological state of the brain is a crucial factor that influences social behavior and interacts with the condition of peripheral organs. To explore the physiological mechanisms underlying caste-specific behaviors in eusocial wasps, we investigated levels of biogenic amines in the brain, lipid storage and ovarian development in the abdomen at different life stages in each caste of the giant hornet Vespa mandarinia. Gynes had significantly larger thoracic widths and more ovarioles than workers. Maximum oocyte lengths and lipid storage differed plastically between life stages, particularly in gynes. At emergence, significantly higher levels of dopamine-related substances were found in the whole brain of gynes than in workers, whereas levels of serotonin-related substances were higher in workers than in gynes. The levels of these substances differed between life stages in each caste. In queenless workers, maximum oocyte lengths were positively correlated with the levels of dopamine-related substances but not positively correlated with other substances we examined. In gynes, dopamine levels in brain sub-compartments were significantly higher than for workers in several regions except for the optic lobes and varied across life stages. These results suggested that dopamine may be associated with the mating and reproductive behavior in gynes, whereas serotonin may be involved in worker-specific behaviors. The dopamine results indicate convergent caste differentiation in brain physiology between eusocial bees and wasps. Biogenic amine dynamics across the life cycle were caste-specific, suggesting different usage between castes.
